abstract: The Burning Glass Institute's July 2025 report finds that for the first time in modern history, a bachelor's degree is no longer a reliable path to professional employment. The report identifies four interlocking structural forces reshaping entry-level work: AI-powered 'Expertise Upheaval' eliminating junior tasks, post-pandemic lean staffing, AI as an accelerant, and a growing graduate glut.
keyFindings: 52% of the Class of 2023 was underemployed a year after graduating
Employment for 22- to 25-year-olds in highly AI-exposed jobs fell by 6% between late 2022 and July 2025
Entry-level postings (less than 3 years of experience) in high-AI-exposure occupations fell from 2022 to 2025, while postings requiring 6+ years held steady or rose
Employers reported plans to hire 7.3% more graduates from the Class of 2025; that expectation had been cut to just 0.6%
By 2034, the U.S. is projected to have nearly 10 million more college-educated workers than jobs that require a degree
methodology: Analysis of job posting data, employment statistics, and employer hiring surveys. The 6% employment decline figure draws on ADP payroll data (via the Brynjolfsson, Chandar, and Chen Stanford study). The 52% underemployment figure is based on tracking college graduates one year post-graduation.
qualifiers: The report identifies four structural forces, not AI alone. The 6% employment decline statistic originates from the Stanford/ADP study rather than independent Burning Glass analysis. The authors note that these changes do not correlate with a larger economic downturn.
